Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)  -- Babies lie side by side in warming beds or sprawled on blankets atop crude wooden tables. Many families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan, seem resigned to the situation. Children with wounds and broken bones are carried in by their parents to wait on stiff plastic chairs. Outside, coughing youngsters squat on the pavement with their anxious families, waiting for care. And everywhere, parents clutch plastic bags containing bring-your-own medicines and supplies. For though they are all awaiting treatment at Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric hospital, the hospital cannot even afford bandages for its patients. The Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in central Kabul has to run on an operating budget of less than $1,200 a month, said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital director. The few supplies that he can buy have to be hoarded for emergencies, and he has to count on parents to buy what's needed to care for their children. "In some cases, there is shortage of the surgical materials, and sometimes we don't have antiseptic to use," Yousufzai said. The United Nations says that more than $15 billion in aid has been sent to Afghanistan since the U.S.-led coalition overthrew the Taliban in late 2001. But still, the hospital cannot afford to help the hundreds of children who stream in every day, desperate for care and cures. The government does pay for salaries and sometimes for fuel, but there is often a shortage of even basic supplies like syringes. Doctors say they have to double up premature babies in incubators. And some of those incubators are compromised. On a recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped onto one machine was the only shield from infection.  Watch scenes from inside the hospital » . The parents waiting anxiously beside their sick children seem resigned to the situation in the hospital. One mother, who declined to give her name, said she spent the family's entire weekly income of $8 on an injection that did not help her baby. "This is something that the hospital should be giving us, because we can't afford it," she said. The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality has dropped by 22 percent since the overthrow of the Taliban but acknowledges that the health status for Afghans is among the worst in the world. One in every five Afghan children will die before their 5th birthday, often of a preventable disease, according to the Save the Children aid agency. The toll on the children and parents is clear to any visitor, and the strain hits the hospital staff, too. "When you see a patient is very, very, sick and you cannot help, and they have to provide something for their children and they are not able to provide, it's also a stress for us," Yousufzai said. At the end of 2001, there were hopes that the hospital would be upgraded, but it is still waiting. It needs some acute care of its own, or it will continue to struggle to help the children who arrive at its door pleading for care.

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) — Infants rest next to one another in heated beds, while others lie on blankets spread over rough wooden tables. At Kabul’s Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital in Afghanistan, many relatives appear to have accepted the harsh conditions as unavoidable.

Parents carry in children suffering from injuries and fractures, then sit with them on hard plastic seats while they wait. Outside the building, young patients with coughs crouch on the sidewalk beside worried family members, also hoping to be seen. Throughout the hospital, mothers and fathers hold plastic bags filled with medicines and medical supplies they have had to bring themselves.

Although everyone there is seeking help at Afghanistan’s only specialized children’s hospital, the facility does not have enough money even to provide bandages. Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital’s director, said the Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, located in central Kabul, operates on less than $1,200 a month.

Because supplies are so limited, the small amount the hospital can purchase must be saved for emergencies. As a result, Yousufzai said, parents are often expected to buy what is needed to treat their children.

“Sometimes there is a shortage of surgical materials, and at times we do not even have antiseptic available,” Yousufzai said.

According to the United Nations, Afghanistan has received more than $15 billion in aid since the U.S.-led coalition removed the Taliban from power in late 2001. Even so, the hospital remains unable to properly treat the hundreds of children who arrive each day in urgent need of medical care.

The Afghan government covers staff salaries and occasionally provides fuel, but even essential items such as syringes are frequently in short supply. Doctors say premature babies sometimes have to share incubators. Some of the incubators themselves are in poor condition. On one recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped to a machine served as the only barrier against infection.

The parents sitting beside their ill children appear anxious but largely resigned to the hospital’s reality. One woman, who did not want to be identified, said she had spent her family’s full weekly income of $8 on an injection that failed to improve her baby’s condition.

“This is something the hospital should provide for us, because we cannot pay for it,” she said.

The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality in Afghanistan has fallen by 22 percent since the Taliban was ousted. However, it also recognizes that Afghans continue to face some of the poorest health conditions in the world.

Save the Children reports that one out of every five Afghan children dies before reaching the age of 5, often from illnesses that could have been prevented.

The suffering of children and their families is obvious to anyone who visits the hospital, and the burden also affects the medical staff.

“When you see a patient who is extremely sick and you cannot help, and the family needs to provide something for the child but cannot afford it, that is stressful for us as well,” Yousufzai said.

At the close of 2001, there had been optimism that the hospital would be improved. Years later, it is still waiting. The facility urgently needs care itself; without it, it will continue struggling to treat the children who come through its doors seeking help.

I can’t reproduce CNN’s exact house style, but here is an original, CNN-like hard-news article draft with a sober, international-news tone. Quotes are written as reported-style placeholders and should be verified before publication.

---

# Kabul children’s hospital overwhelmed as Afghanistan’s health crisis deepens

**Kabul, Afghanistan** — In the dim corridors of Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, Afghanistan’s largest pediatric facility, mothers sit shoulder to shoulder beside metal beds, cradling children weakened by pneumonia, malnutrition and preventable infections.

Some infants share oxygen points. Others lie under thin blankets while relatives search for medicines outside the hospital because the pharmacy shelves are bare. Doctors say they are treating far more children than the hospital was built to handle — and with far fewer supplies than they need.

“We are receiving children in critical condition every day, but we do not have enough medicine, oxygen, antibiotics or even basic equipment,” the hospital director said. “Our doctors are doing everything they can, but the needs are far beyond our capacity.”

The hospital, located in central Kabul, has long served as a lifeline for families from across Afghanistan. But staff say the pressure has become increasingly severe as poverty, food insecurity and the collapse of large parts of the health system push more children into emergency care.

## Parents arrive with nowhere else to go

Many families say they traveled for hours — sometimes days — to reach Kabul after local clinics either turned them away or lacked medicine.

“My son had a fever and could not breathe,” said one father from Logar province, standing beside his child’s hospital bed. “The clinic near our home told us to come here, but when we arrived, they told us we must buy some medicine ourselves. I do not have money left.”

A mother from Wardak province said her 8-month-old daughter had been losing weight for weeks.

“She cries but has no strength,” the mother said. “The doctors say she needs special milk and medicine. Sometimes they have it, sometimes they do not. We are just waiting and praying.”

Hospital staff say such cases are now routine. Children arrive suffering from complications linked to hunger, unsafe drinking water, cold weather and delayed treatment. Many are underweight. Some are too weak to respond quickly to care.

## Shortages of basic medical supplies

Doctors and nurses at the hospital say they are short of some of the most basic items needed to treat children, including:

- Injectable antibiotics  
- Oxygen supplies and functioning oxygen equipment  
- IV fluids and cannulas  
- Pediatric feeding tubes  
- Therapeutic milk for severely malnourished children  
- Gloves, syringes and disinfectant  
- Nebulizers and respiratory medicines  
- Blood bags and laboratory reagents  
- Fuel for generators and heating  

In some wards, families are asked to buy prescriptions from private pharmacies outside the hospital — an impossible demand for many Afghans living on little or no income.

“If a child needs an antibiotic and we do not have it, the family must find it outside,” one doctor said. “But many parents cannot afford even the transport to come here. How can they pay for medicine?”

## A national crisis reflected in one hospital

Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis remains one of the world’s most severe. According to UN agencies, more than **23 million people** in the country need humanitarian assistance in 2024, including millions of children. Aid groups have warned that funding shortfalls have forced cuts to health, nutrition and food programs across the country.

The World Food Programme has said funding gaps have reduced its ability to support vulnerable families, while UNICEF has repeatedly warned that Afghan children face heightened risks from malnutrition, disease and lack of access to health care.

Health workers say the consequences are visible in the pediatric wards of Kabul.

“This hospital shows the condition of the whole country,” the director said. “When families cannot buy food, when clinics close, when mothers cannot get care during pregnancy, the children come to us — often too late.”

## Doctors stretched thin

Despite the shortages, staff continue to work long shifts. Nurses move quickly between crowded beds, adjusting IV lines and checking fevers. Doctors say they often must decide which child receives limited oxygen equipment first.

“There are moments when we have more children needing oxygen than oxygen points available,” a senior physician said. “No doctor should have to make that choice.”

The hospital’s intensive care areas are particularly strained. Children with severe pneumonia, sepsis, congenital conditions and acute malnutrition compete for limited beds. In some rooms, two patients share space meant for one.

Parents remain at bedsides around the clock, feeding children, holding oxygen masks in place and helping nurses clean bedding.

“We cannot leave,” said one mother whose son was being treated for a respiratory infection. “If he needs something, I must be here. But I have other children at home, and they also need food.”

## Aid groups warn of worsening conditions

International aid organizations say Afghanistan’s health system has struggled since the Taliban returned to power in 2021 and foreign development funding was sharply reduced. While humanitarian support has kept some facilities operating, aid officials say emergency funding cannot replace a functioning national health system.

Cuts to nutrition programs are especially dangerous for children, experts warn. Malnutrition weakens immune systems, making common illnesses such as diarrhea and pneumonia more deadly.

At Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, doctors say they fear the winter months, when respiratory illnesses rise and poor families struggle to heat their homes.

“When the weather gets colder, we see more pneumonia, more burns from unsafe heating, more malnutrition,” the hospital director said. “Without urgent support, more children will die from conditions that can be treated.”

## Families wait, hoping for recovery

In one ward, a father gently rubbed his daughter’s feet as she slept beneath a blanket. He said he had borrowed money for the trip to Kabul and did not know how he would repay it.

“I only want her to live,” he said. “If there is medicine, she can get better. If there is no medicine, what can we do?”

For Afghanistan’s doctors, that question has become painfully familiar.

“We need medicine. We need equipment. We need support for these children,” the director said. “They should not die because a hospital does not have the basics.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Afghanistan’s only specialist pediatric hospital overwhelmed as sick children arrive faster than doctors can treat them**

*KABUL —* In the crowded corridors of Afghanistan’s main children’s hospital, mothers sit shoulder to shoulder on thin blankets, cradling feverish babies while waiting for a bed that may not become available. Some children breathe through oxygen tubes shared between wards. Others lie two to a mattress as nurses move quickly between patients, trying to stretch limited medicine, staff and equipment across a daily wave of emergencies.

The Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital in Kabul, long regarded as Afghanistan’s only specialist pediatric referral hospital, has become a stark symbol of the country’s fragile health system. Despite billions of dollars in international assistance poured into Afghanistan after the fall of the Taliban regime in 2001, the hospital continues to struggle with shortages of supplies, trained staff, functioning equipment and space.

Doctors say many children arrive critically ill after travelling for hours — sometimes days — from rural provinces where clinics are poorly stocked or no longer functioning adequately. Pneumonia, malnutrition, diarrhea, measles complications, heart defects and premature birth are among the leading reasons for admission.

“We receive far more patients than this hospital was built to handle,” one pediatric doctor said. “By the time many families reach us, the child is already in a severe condition.”

Afghanistan has received enormous international aid over the past two decades, including funds intended to rebuild hospitals, train health workers and expand basic services. But health officials and aid workers say much of the system remained dependent on foreign funding, with uneven investment, weak infrastructure, corruption, insecurity and shortages of trained personnel undermining long-term progress.

The situation worsened after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, when many donors suspended or redirected development assistance. Humanitarian agencies stepped in to keep essential services running, but funding gaps have persisted. Sanctions-related banking restrictions, the departure of many skilled professionals and limits on women’s work in some sectors have further complicated the delivery of health care.

At the children’s hospital, the consequences are visible. Families are often asked to buy medicines from private pharmacies because hospital stocks are insufficient. Diagnostic machines may be broken or overused. Intensive care beds are limited, and doctors must make painful decisions about which children receive priority treatment.

For poor families, the cost of care can be devastating even when consultations are nominally free. Many parents borrow money for transport, medicine and food while staying in Kabul. Some sell livestock or household goods to keep a child alive.

“My son was sick for two weeks before we could come here,” said one mother from a northern province, holding a malnourished toddler wrapped in a scarf. “The clinic near our village had no medicine. We came because people said this hospital treats children, but there are so many patients.”

Aid agencies warn that Afghanistan’s child health crisis is being driven not only by hospital shortages but also by poverty, hunger, poor sanitation and low vaccination coverage in some areas. Repeated droughts, economic collapse and restrictions on livelihoods have left millions of families unable to afford nutritious food or timely medical care.

The United Nations and international relief organizations have repeatedly appealed for sustained funding to prevent the collapse of Afghanistan’s health system. But humanitarian support is often short-term, focused on emergency relief rather than rebuilding durable national services.

Health workers at the Kabul hospital say they continue to do what they can, but they describe a system operating beyond its limits.

“This hospital saves many lives,” a senior nurse said. “But every day we see children who could have been saved earlier if there were better clinics, better roads, more medicine and more doctors in the provinces.”

For Afghanistan’s sickest children, the hospital remains a last hope. Yet its overcrowded wards show how far the country still is from providing reliable health care to its youngest patients — even after years of international promises and billions spent in aid.

counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL — At Afghanistan’s largest children’s hospital, doctors improvise as funding falls short**

KABUL, Afghanistan — In the crowded corridors of Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, the country’s main pediatric referral facility, the scale of need is visible before a doctor says a word: families sitting on floors beside bundled infants, mothers holding IV bags above their children’s beds, and nurses moving quickly between wards where basic supplies run out too often.

Hospital staff say the monthly operating budget is about **$1,200** — a sum that barely covers the needs of a facility receiving some of Afghanistan’s sickest children. In several wards, doctors and nurses describe shortages of essentials including **bandages and antiseptic**, forcing staff to ration supplies or ask families to purchase what they can from outside pharmacies.

“We treat children every day knowing we do not have enough,” said one medical worker at the hospital, speaking amid a steady stream of patients arriving from Kabul and surrounding provinces. “Sometimes the medicine is not here. Sometimes even the simplest materials are not here.”

In the neonatal unit, the pressure is especially acute. **Premature babies share incubators**, a practice doctors say is dangerous but, in the absence of enough functioning equipment, sometimes unavoidable. Tiny newborns lie side by side beneath warming lights as staff try to monitor infections, breathing problems and low birth weight complications with limited equipment.

For families, the hospital is often the last hope. Many have traveled long distances after local clinics failed to provide treatment, or after they could no longer afford private care. Parents describe selling household items or borrowing money for transport, medicine and food during hospital stays.

The strain comes as Afghanistan continues to face some of the world’s gravest child health challenges. According to international child-health estimates, **tens of thousands of Afghan children die each year before reaching age five**, many from preventable or treatable causes including neonatal complications, pneumonia, diarrhea and malnutrition. Afghanistan’s under-five mortality rate remains among the highest in the region, and doctors say poverty, food insecurity and weakened public services are driving more critically ill children to Kabul.

Inside Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, the statistics are reflected in daily choices: which child gets oxygen first, how long a baby can remain in an incubator, whether a family can afford antibiotics, whether a nurse can find clean gauze for a dressing.

Health workers say they are doing what they can, but the gap between need and resources is widening. Without consistent funding for supplies, equipment, salaries and nutrition support, they warn, the hospital will continue to operate in crisis mode.

“This hospital carries the burden of children from across the country,” said another staff member. “But a children’s hospital cannot run on sympathy alone.”

counterfactuals.output:
KABUL, Afghanistan — In the crowded corridors of a children’s hospital in Kabul, the day begins before sunrise.

Mothers wrapped in shawls sit shoulder to shoulder on metal benches, holding feverish infants against their chests. Fathers stand in long lines clutching medical papers and handwritten prescriptions. Children cough, cry or lie quietly under blankets brought from home, their small bodies weakened by pneumonia, malnutrition or infections that might have been treated earlier — if their families had been able to afford transport, medicine or a doctor closer to home.

Inside one ward, two children share a bed. In another, nurses move quickly between patients, checking IV lines and oxygen tubes, while anxious relatives wait just outside the door. The hospital is one of the few places many families believe they can still find help. But even here, doctors say, the system is under extraordinary strain.

“We are receiving more patients than we have capacity for,” one health worker said. “Many arrive very late, because their families have no money or no clinic nearby.”

The pressure inside Kabul’s pediatric hospitals reflects a deepening crisis across Afghanistan’s health sector — a crisis driven by poverty, shrinking international aid, shortages of medicine and staff, and the long-term effects of decades of war.

For years, Afghanistan’s public health system depended heavily on foreign funding. International donors supported hospitals, vaccination campaigns, maternal health services and clinics in remote districts. But since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, much of that funding has been reduced, frozen or redirected through humanitarian channels rather than government systems.

Aid agencies have kept many services running, but they warn the support is not enough. Hospitals face recurring shortages of essential drugs, fuel, laboratory supplies and salaries. Some facilities rely on temporary funding cycles, making it difficult to plan or retain staff. Others have reduced services or asked patients’ families to buy medicine privately — a near-impossible demand in a country where millions are struggling to afford food.

The result is visible in Kabul’s waiting rooms. Families travel from distant provinces after local clinics run out of supplies or cannot treat serious cases. Many arrive with children suffering from conditions made worse by malnutrition, poor sanitation, cold weather and delayed care.

Afghanistan is also facing one of the world’s largest humanitarian emergencies. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that millions of Afghans need assistance, with children among the most vulnerable. Malnutrition remains widespread, and outbreaks of preventable diseases pose a constant threat in communities with limited access to clean water, vaccines and basic medical services.

Women and girls face additional barriers. Taliban restrictions on female education and employment have affected the pipeline of future female health workers, while in many conservative areas, women may be reluctant or unable to seek treatment from male doctors. Aid groups say preserving female participation in health care is essential, especially for maternal and child health.

Doctors in Kabul say they are doing what they can with limited resources. But they describe a system stretched beyond its limits: too many patients, too few beds, too little money and a growing number of families who cannot pay for care outside public hospitals.

In the pediatric wards, the crisis is measured in quiet, intimate moments — a mother fanning her child’s face, a father counting the last of his cash for medicine, a nurse trying to comfort three families at once.

For many Afghans, the hospital remains a place of hope. But as funding gaps widen and needs grow, that hope is becoming harder to sustain.

**Afghan Parents Forced to Buy Medicines, Supplies for Children at Kabul’s Main Pediatric Hospital**

*KABUL, Afghanistan —* At Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, Afghanistan’s largest pediatric referral facility, the burden of keeping sick children alive is increasingly falling on parents who can least afford it.

Families arriving from Kabul and far-flung provinces say they are being asked to purchase medicines, syringes, IV fluids, laboratory supplies and even basic items needed for treatment outside the hospital, often from nearby private pharmacies. For many, the costs come after days of travel, lost wages and mounting debt — and amid an economic crisis that has left millions of Afghans dependent on humanitarian aid.

Parents interviewed at the hospital described a familiar routine: a doctor examines a child and writes a prescription, but the family must leave the ward to buy the required drugs or supplies before treatment can continue. Some say they borrow money from relatives, sell household goods or delay care while searching for cheaper medicines.

“My child needed injections and serum, but the hospital did not have them,” said one father from an outlying province, holding a small plastic bag of medicines purchased at a pharmacy near the hospital. “We came here because we thought treatment would be free. Now every day there is something else to buy.”

Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital has long been a critical lifeline for Afghan families, treating children with malnutrition, pneumonia, sepsis, congenital conditions, trauma injuries and other serious illnesses. But the facility has been under severe pressure as Afghanistan’s health system struggles with funding shortfalls, staff shortages, overcrowding and supply disruptions.

Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, a senior official at the hospital, has pointed to the scale of demand and the limits of available resources, saying the hospital continues to treat large numbers of children despite shortages of medicines and equipment. He said doctors and nurses are working under difficult conditions, while many essential supplies depend on external support and irregular deliveries.

The crisis reflects a broader breakdown in health financing since international development assistance to Afghanistan sharply contracted following the Taliban’s return to power in 2021. Before that, much of the country’s public health system relied heavily on donor funding, including support linked to the United States Agency for International Development, or USAID, as well as other international partners.

Aid groups say the loss or reduction of predictable development funding has left hospitals and clinics unable to consistently provide free care, even as poverty, hunger and disease have intensified. The United Nations has repeatedly warned that Afghanistan’s humanitarian needs remain among the world’s highest, with children bearing the heaviest burden.

U.N. agencies have reported that millions of Afghan children face acute food insecurity, and many are vulnerable to preventable diseases because of weak access to health care, clean water and nutrition services. At pediatric wards in Kabul, doctors say malnutrition often complicates otherwise treatable illnesses, making recovery slower and more dangerous.

Save the Children has also warned that Afghanistan’s children are being pushed deeper into crisis by poverty, collapsing services and reduced aid. The organization has urged donors not to abandon Afghan families, saying cuts in humanitarian funding can quickly translate into fewer medicines, fewer functioning clinics and more preventable deaths.

Inside Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, the consequences are visible in crowded corridors and anxious waiting rooms. Mothers sit beside children connected to oxygen or IV lines. Fathers move between wards and pharmacies, clutching prescriptions and counting cash. Some families say they were referred to Kabul only after local clinics could not provide care.

For families already living on the edge, even small medical expenses can become impossible. A course of antibiotics, a scan, a blood test or a few days of IV fluids may cost more than a family earns in weeks. When hospitals lack supplies, the poorest patients are often the first to suffer.

Health workers say the hospital still provides consultations and emergency care, but shortages mean families are frequently asked to help obtain items that should ordinarily be stocked by the facility. Doctors describe an impossible situation: children need urgent treatment, but hospital stores are depleted and outside assistance is not enough to meet demand.

Dr. Yousufzai said the hospital needs sustained support for medicines, diagnostic equipment, nutrition programs and basic consumables. He emphasized that the facility remains committed to treating children, but that doctors cannot do it alone without dependable supplies and funding.

Humanitarian organizations say Afghanistan’s health system requires both immediate emergency assistance and longer-term investment. Short-term aid can keep wards functioning, but without stable financing, hospitals will continue to run out of essential medicines and families will continue paying out of pocket.

For parents at Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, the debate over aid mechanisms and donor policy feels painfully distant. Their concerns are immediate: finding the next vial, the next test, the next meal — and keeping their children alive.

“I will do anything for my child,” one mother said, sitting beside her son’s hospital bed. “But if we have no money, what can we do?”
